title: Equations Like p(x + q) = r
short: Divide first, or distribute first; both work.
trouble: Students distribute to the first term only, or add q before dividing.

blocks.html: Some equations have a group in parentheses, like $3(x + 4) = 27$. You can solve them with two steps, or distribute first. Both roads lead to the same answer.
For $p(x + q) = r$: either divide both sides by $p$ first and then undo the $q$, or distribute first ($px + pq = r$) and solve the two-step equation.

In $3(x + 4)$, the order of operations says: add 4 to $x$, then multiply the whole group by 3. Undo in reverse: divide by 3, then subtract 4. Distributing first is also fine, because $3(x + 4)$ and $3x + 12$ are equal for every $x$.

steps: 3(x + 4) = 27: three equal groups, each x + 4, make 27.

blocks.title: Two ways with a negative
steps: Or distribute first: $-2x + 10 = 18$, so $-2x = 8$ and $x = -4$. Same answer.

blocks.title: A fraction outside
steps: Multiply both sides by the reciprocal $\frac{4}{3}$: $x + 8 = 9 \times \frac{4}{3} = 12$.

blocks.html: Distributing to the first term only ($3(x + 4) = 27$ becoming $3x + 4 = 27$), or subtracting 4 before dividing ($3(x + 4) = 27$ becoming $3x = 23$). The 4 is inside the group, so it is multiplied by 3 too. Check your answer in the original equation.
